The theory of sets is a hugely important basis for many other areas of mathematics, with a long history.

Definition 1.1 - Set

A set is a collection of objects. The objects belonging to a set are called elements or members of the set. We might define the elements in a set by listing them (sometimes called tabular form), or stating a property they all share. A set has no duplicates, and the order of the objects in the set is not important.S = \{ a, b, c \} \qquad \mathbb{N} = \{ 1,2,3,4 \ldots\} \qquad X = \{ x \in \mathbb{N}: 1 \leq x \leq 10 \}

Sets are usually denoted by capital letters and set elements are denoted by lower case letters.
The symbol \in is used to denote ‘is an element of’ or ‘belongs to’ or ‘a member of’.

The elements of a set can be written in a list, separated by commas, in between a pair of set brackets: \{ \}. (This is sometimes called roster notation.)

We need sets to be well-defined, which means it should always be possible from the definition of a set to decide whether a given element belongs to the set or not.

Example 1.1

Which of the following are well-defined sets?

(i) Let A be the set of all whole numbers greater than 0

(ii) Let B be the set of all numbers funkier than 8

(iii) Let C be the set of numbers that are both odd and even.

(iv) Let D be the set of all numbers that are in the set D

(iv) Let E be the set of numbers where the sum of the numbers in the set is 10.

Solution

(i) This is well-defined.

(ii) This is not well-defined, as funkiness is not a subjective property of numbers that can be evaluated unambiguously.

(iii) This is well-defined, as I can tell you whether any given number belongs in the set not (but the answer is no for all numbers!)

(iv) This is not well-defined, as I cannot say whether a particular number is in the set or not without more information.

(iv) This is not well-defined, as it does not define a unique set.

Theorem 1.1 - The Axiom of Extensionality

Two sets A and B are equal if and only if A and B contain the same elements.

A set is completely defined by its elements

The order the elements are listed in the set is irrelevant

If the same element is listed more than once, the additional instances can be ignoredS = \{ a, b, c \} = \{ a, c, b \} = \{ a, b, b, c, c,c,c,c \}

Definition 1.3 - Subset

A subset is a set whose elements are contained in a larger set. We say A is a subset of B, denoted A \subseteq B, if every element of A is also an element in B.A \subseteq B\quad \Leftrightarrow\quad x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B\quad \Leftrightarrow\quad B \supseteq A

We can also say that B is a superset of A.

If A is not a subset of B - that is, there is at least one element of A which does not belong to B - then we write A \not\subseteq B.

A proper subset is a subset which is not equal to the larger set - we write A \subset B, or say ‘A is properly contained in B’, if there is at least one element of B not in A.A \subset B\quad \Leftrightarrow\quad x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B, A \neq B

Note

This notation follows the same rule as the <, >, \leq, \geq symbols we use for ‘less than’ versus ‘less than or equal to’, etc. The second line under the symbol mimics the = symbol.

For example,

P = \{x\}, T = \{x, y, z\} and M = \{v, w, x, y, z\} are subsets of L = \{v, w, x, y, z\}. P and T are proper subsets. Therefore, we may write
P \subset L \textrm{, }\qquad T\subset L \quad \textrm{ and }\quad M\subseteq L

S_1 = \{1,2,3\} and S_2 = \{1,2\}. Then S_2 \subseteq S_1 but S_1 \not\subset S_2.

\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z}, since every natural number is also an integer. Also, \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q}, since every integer is also a rational number (e.g. 3 = \frac{3}{1}), and \mathbb{Q}
\subset \mathbb{R}, since every rational number is also a real number.

Example 1.3

(a) Write down all the possible subsets of A= \{ 1,2,3\}.

(b) Let S_1 = \{ 5, 12 \}, S_2 = \{ 5, 12, 13 \} and S_3 = \{ 5,14 \}. Which of the following are true?

  i) S_1 \subset S_2

  ii) S_1 \subseteq S_2

  iii) S_1 \subseteq S_1

  iv) S_2\subset S_1

  v) S_2 \supseteq S_1

  vi) S_3 \subset S_2

  vii) S_1 = S_2

(c) Write down an expression relating \mathbb{C}, \mathbb{N}, \mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R} and \mathbb{Z} (using the \subset symbol four times).

Solution

a) The subsets of A = \{1,2,3\} are \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}, \{1,2,3\}.

b)

  i) S_1 \subset S_2 - true, as everything in S_1 is also in S_2 (but there are elements of S_2 not in S_1).

  ii) S_1 \subseteq S_2 - true, as everything in S_1 is also in S_2; this must be true if S_1 \subset S_2

  iii) S_1 \subseteq S_1 - true, as everything in S_1 is also in S_1; this is true of any set, as it equals itself

  iv) S_2\subset S_1  - false, as 13 \not\in S_1

  v) S_2 \supseteq S_1 - true, as this is the same statement as S_1 \subseteq S_2

  vi) S_3 \subset S_2 - false, as 14 \not\in S_2

  vii) S_1 = S_2 - false, as 13 \not\in S_1

c) \mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}.

Theorem 1.2 - Properties of subsets

For any set A, we have A \subseteq A.

If A \subseteq B and B \subseteq C, then A \subseteq C.

Definition 1.4 - The universal set

The universal set, denoted by U, is a set containing all  is a set containing all the elements of all sets under consideration. For example, if we are working with sets of real numbers, U = \mathbb{R}.

If we are studying human populations, the universal set consists of all the people in the world.

In plane geometry, the universal set consists of all points in the plane.

We could define U to be the set of whole numbers from 1 to 10 (i.e. U=\{1, 2, 3, \cdots
9, 10\}), and then only consider sets which are subsets of U.

Definition 1.5 - The empty set

The empty set, sometimes also called the null set, is a set containing no elements. It can be denoted by \{\} or \varnothing.

For example,\{x\ |\ x \in \mathbb{N}, x < 0\} = \varnothing

Definition 1.6 - Unit set

A unit set is a set containing only a single element. For example, S = \{x\}.

Let A = {2,4,5} and B = {1,4,6,8} Then, A ⋂ B = {4}.

Theorem 1.3 - Properties of the universal and empty sets

\varnothing is a subset of every set A, and a proper subset of every set A \neq \varnothing.

For any set A, we have \varnothing \subseteq A \subseteq U.

Definition 1.7 - Set equality

Two sets A and B are equal (denoted A=B), if and only if they have exactly the same elements. That is, each member of A is a member of B, and vice versa.A = B\quad \Leftrightarrow\quad A \subseteq B, B \subseteq A

For example,

\{ \textrm{Prolog, Lisp, Modula2, Java, C}\} = \{\textrm{Lisp, Modula2, C, Prolog, Java}\}

\{3, 6, 9, 12, \ldots\}=\{x \in \mathbb{Z}\ |\ x=3m, m \in \mathbb{N}\}.

\{x \in A\ |\ x\textrm{ is a vowel}\} = \{a, e, i, o, u\} (where A is the set of letters in the alphabet)

\{2, 3, 4\} = \{x\ |\ x\textrm{ is a digit in the numeral } 23432\}

Example 1.4

Which of the following statements about sets are true?

(i) \{ 1,2,3 \} = \{ 1, 2, 2, 3\}

(ii) \{6,7\} = \{7,6\}

(iii) \{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \ |\ 2 < x < 6 \} = \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}

(iv) \mathbb{Z} = \{x+1 \ |\ x \in \mathbb{Z}\}

(v) \mathbb{N} = \{x+1 \ |\ x \in \mathbb{N}\}

Solution

(i) These sets are equal.

(ii) These sets are equal.

(iii) These sets are not equal, as the left-hand set does not contain 2 or 6.

(iv) These sets are equal.

(v) These sets are not equal, since 1 is not in the right-hand set but it is in \mathbb{N}.

Theorem 1.4 - Properties of set equality

For any set A, A = A.

If A = B, then B = A

If A = B and B = C, then A = C.

A = B \Leftrightarrow A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A.

Named after 19th-century mathematician John Venn, Venn diagrams are an extremely useful way to visualise sets and their properties and relations.



All Venn diagrams are enclose in a rectangle which represents the universal set U - all the points inside the rectangle are in U.





Defined subsets of U are represented by a circle or ellipse drawn inside the rectangle.





Here we can see the set A, represented by the points inside the rectangle, and the complement of A (A^\mathsf{c} = U \setminus A).

If we have multiple subsets within U, they are drawn as overlapping, so we can define the set of points that lie in both sets, and have a region to represent it. The regions can be labelled inside the circle, or outside just next to the line (as long as it’s clear what you mean).





Example 1.6

Use a Venn diagram to display the sets A = \{1,2,3,4\} and B = \{3,4,5,6\}.

Solution





We can also construct Venn diagrams for larger numbers of overlapping sets, and label each region to show which sets overlap there. For 3 sets, it’s still possible to use circles.





But for 4 circles there’s no way to arrange them so that all overlapping sections are present:





In the diagram above, there is no region to represent AD or BC. It is possible to construct such a diagram using ellipses:





As an alternative to Venn diagrams, we use the term Euler diagram to describe a diagram where not all overlaps are present. This may be desirable, especially if some are empty, or if including them all would make the diagram too complicated. The four-set example above made from circles is an example of an Euler diagram.

Euler diagrams have a little more flexibility - for example, if one set is a proper subset of another, its circle can be drawn inside another set.





As we develop more terminology to describe sets and their relationships, we will be able to use Venn diagrams to illustrate them and to help us make sense of how the sets are related.

Example 1.7





Sketch copies of the diagram above, and shade the regions corresponding to:

(i) A

(ii) A^\mathsf{c}

(iii) A \setminus B

Solution

(i) A





(ii) A^\mathsf{c}





(iii) A \setminus B
There are various operations we can perform to compare and combine sets, and observe the relationships between them.

Definition 1.11 - Intersection

The intersection of two sets A and B, denoted A \cap B, is the set of elements that lie in both A and B. That is,A \cap B = \{x\ |\ x \in A \textrm{ and } x \in B\}





For example,

Let A = \{2,4,5\} and B = \{1,4,6,8\} Then A \cap B = \{4\}.

Let A = \{2,4,5\} and B = \{1,3\}. Then A \cap B = \varnothing.

Note

If a set contains only a single element, it is sometimes called a singleton set or unit set.

If two sets do not intersect, we say they have an empty intersection, and write A \cap B = \varnothing.

Definition 1.12 - Symmetric Difference

The symmetric difference of two sets A and B, denoted A \oplus B, is the set of elements that lie in one of A or B but not in both - that is, A \oplus B = \{ x\ |\ x \in A \cup B, x \not\in A \cap B \}. We can write:A \oplus B = (A \cup B) \setminus (A \cap B) = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)





For example,

Let U = \mathbb{N} be the universal set, and let A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, B = \{3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}, C = \{2, 3, 8, 9\}, and let E = \{2, 4, 6, 8, \ldots\} be the even numbers. Then
A \oplus B = \{1, 2, 5, 6, 7\} \qquad B \oplus C = \{2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\} \qquad A \oplus C = \{ 1, 4, 8, 9\}


And A \oplus E = \{1, 3, 6, 8, 10, \ldots \}
(this is the infinite set of even numbers, but with 2 and 4 replaced by 1 and 3).

The operations \cup, \cap and \setminus can be repeated or combined to derive more sets. We can use brackets to specify the order in which operations must be performed.

Example 1.8

Let A = \{1,2,3,4\}, B= \{3,4,5,6,7\} and C = \{6,7,8\}. Write in list form:

(i) (A \cup B) \cap C

(ii) (A \cup C) \setminus (B\cup C)

Solution

(i) (A \cup B) \cap C = \{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\} \cap \{6,7,8\} = \{6,7\}

(ii) (A \cup C) \setminus (B\cup C) = \{1,2,3,4,6,7,8\} \setminus \{3,4,5,6,7,8\} = \{1,2\}

Definition 1.13 - Disjoint sets

Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint or non-intersecting if they have no elements in common - or, using
the definition of intersection, A and B are disjoint if A \cap B = \varnothing, the empty set.

If S = A \cup B and A \cap B = \varnothing, we say S is the disjoint union of A and $B.

Theorem 1.5 - Properties of unions and intersections

For two sets A and B, we have:

Every element X in A \cap B belongs to both A and B; hence
x \in A \cap B \Rightarrow x \in A \textrm{ and } x \in B

A \cap B is a subset of A and a subset of B; that is,
A \cap B \subseteq A \qquad A \cap B \subseteq B

Every element X in A \cup B belongs to either A or B; hence
x \in A \cap B \Rightarrow x \in A \textrm{ or } x \in B

A and B are both subsets of A \cup B; that is,
A \subseteq A \cup \qquad B \subseteq A \cup B

The number of elements in a set, or the size of the set, is an important property of the set.

Definition 1.7 - Finite and infinite sets

A set is finite if it is empty, or if it consists of exactly n distinct elements where n is a positive integer; otherwise it is infinite.

A set is countable if it is finite, or if it has infinitely many elements which can be ordered in a sequence, in which case S is said to be countably infinite; otherwise the set is uncountable.

Example 1.9

For each of the following sets, say whether it is finite, countably infinite or uncountably infinite.

(i) Let M be the set of the days of the week; that is,M = \{\textrm{Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday}\}

(ii) P = \{x\ |\ x \textrm{ is a river on the surface of the Earth}\}.

(iii) Let Y be the set of (positive) even integers, i.e. Y = \{2, 4, 6, \ldots \}

(iv) Let I be the unit interval of the real numbers, i.e. I = \{x\in\mathbb{R}\ |\ 0 \leq 𝑥 \leq 1\}

Solution

(i) M is a finite set, as it contains 7 elements.

(ii) Although it may difficult to count, P is a finite set.

(iii) Y is a countably infinite set.

(iv) I is an uncountably infinite set.

Theorem 1.6 - Countability of the Rational Numbers

The set of rational numbers, \mathbb{Q} = \{ \frac{p}{q} \ |\ p, q \in \mathbb{R}\}, is a countably infinite set.

Proof proof goes here

Definition 1.7 - Set Cardinality

The cardinality of a finite set A is the number of elements that it contains, or the size of the set. The cardinality of A is denoted by n(A) or |A|.

For example,

Let A be the set of odd positive integers less than 10. Then n(A)=|A| = 5.

Let S be the set of letters in the English alphabet. Then n(S)=|S| = 26.

Because the empty set has no elements, we have n(\varnothing) = 0.

Theorem 1.7 - Cardinality of combined sets

If A and B are finite disjoint sets, then A \cup B is finite andn(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B)

If A \subset U, a finite universal set, then U is the disjoint union of A and its
complement A^\mathsf{c}. Thenn(U) = n(A) + n(A^\mathsf{c}) \qquad \textrm{ and } \qquad n(A^\mathsf{c}) = n(U) - n(A)

If A and B are finite sets, thenn(A\setminus B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)

For example,

If there are 2 goth members in a band of 5 musicians, then there are 5 – 2 = 3 non-goth band members.

Suppose an archery class A contains 35 students, and 15 of them are also in a bowling class B. Thenn(A \setminus B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B) = 35 - 15 = 20

Testing cardinality of combined sets

Determining the cardinality of unions of non-disjoint sets is slightly harder, as the size of the union will depend on to what extent the sets overlap.

Theorem 1.8 - Inclusion-Exclusion Principle

Suppose A and B are finite sets, not necessarily disjoint. Then A \cap B and A \cup B are finite, andn(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)

That is, we find the number of elements that are in A or B (or both) by first adding n(A) and n(B) (inclusion), and then subtracting n(A\cap B) (exclusion) - since the elements in A\cap B were counted twice, we need to remove them from the total.





Suppose A, B and C are finite sets. Then A \cup B \cup C is finite and\begin{align*}
n(A \cup B \cup C) &= n(A) + n(B) + n(C) \\
 &- n(A \cap B)- n(B \cap C) - n(A \cap C)\\& + n(A \cap B \cap C)
\end{align*}

Once we have the notion of as set, we can construct different kinds of sets - including sets which contain other sets, and use them to describe structures in mathematics. For example, if we consider a set of lines, each element is itself a set of points.

Definition 1.8 - Power set

The power set of a set A is the set of all possible subsets of A (including the set itself, and the empty set). The power set of A is denoted by P(A).P(A) = \{x\ |\ x \subseteq A\}

If A is a finite set and has k elements, then P(A) will have 2^k elements.n(A) = k \quad \Rightarrow \quad n(P(A)) = 2^k

For example: Let A=\{a, b, c\}. Then P(A)=\{\varnothing, \{a\},\{b\}, \{c\}, \{a, b\}, \{a, c\}, \{b, c\}, A\}

Example 1.13

(i)  Let A = \{ h, k \}. Write down P(A) and n(P(A)).

(ii)  Let B = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4 \}. Write down P(B) and n(P(B)).

(iii) What is the power set of the empty set \varnothing?

(iv) What is the power set of \{\varnothing\}?

Solution

(i) P(A) = \{ \varnothing, \{1\}, \{2\}, A\}, which contains 

22 = 4 elements.

(ii) P(B) = \{ \varnothing, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{4\}, \{1,2\}, \{1,3\},\{1,4\}, \{2,3\},
  \{2,4\}, \{3,4\}, \{1,2,3\}, \{1,2,4\}, \{1,3,4\}, \{2,3,4\}, B\}, which contains 

24 = 16 elements.

(iii) The empty set has exactly one subset, namely, itself. So, P(\varnothing) = \{\varnothing\}, and n(P(\varnothing))=2^0=1.

(iv) The set \{\varnothing\} has exactly two subsets, namely, \varnothing and the set \{\varnothing\} itself. Therefore
P(\{\varnothing\})=\{ \varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\} and n(P(\{\varnothing)\})=2^1=2.

Definition 1.8 - Partition

The partition of a set A is a subdivision of A into nonempty subsets which are disjoint and whose union is A. That is, a set of nonempty subsets of A such that each a \in A belongs to exactly one of the subsets.

Let S be a non-empty set, and define P = \{ S_1, S_2, \ldots S_n\} where S_i \subseteq S for each i. Then P is a partition of S if:

S_i \neq \varnothing for each i

The subsets are pairwise disjoint; that is, S_i \cap S_j = \varnothing if i \neq j.

The union of the subsets S_i is the set S; that is, S_1 \cup S_2 \cup \ldots \cup S_n = S.

Note

For the final condition above, we can also write:\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} S_i = S

For example, if S = \{a,b,c\}, then P = \{\{a,b\},\{c\}\} is a partition of S.

Theorem 1.8 - Duality of set equations

Let E be an equation in set algebra. TThe dual E* of E is the equation obtained by replacing each occurrence of \cup with \cap and vice versa, and each occurrence of U with \varnothing and vice versa.

If E is a true statement about sets, then its dual E* is also true.

For example, we know (U \cap A) \cup (B \cap A) = A. By duality, we also know that (\varnothing \cup A) \cap (B \cup A) = A

The following properties and relationships hold for set operations.

Complement laws:A \cup A^\mathsf{c} = U \qquad  A \cap A^\mathsf{c} = \varnothing

Identity lawsA \cap U = A \qquad A cup \varnothing = A

Domination lawsA \cup U = U \qquad A \cap \varnothing = \varnothing

Idempotent lawsA \cup A = A \qquad A \cap A = \varnothing

Double complement law(A^\mathsf{c})^\mathsf{c} = A

Commutative lawsA \cup B = B \cup A \qquad A \cap B = B \cap A

Absorption lawsA \cup (A \cap B) = A \qquad A \cap (A \cup B) = A

Associative laws(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C) = A \cup B \cup C

(A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C) = A \cap B \cap C

Distributive lawsA \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C) \qquad A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)

A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C) \qquad A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)

De Morgan’s laws(A \cup B)^\mathsf{c} = A^\mathsf{c} \cap B^\mathsf{c} \qquad (A \cap B)^\mathsf{c} = A^\mathsf{c} \cup B^\mathsf{c}

An important example of a Cartesian product is given by the set of Cartesian coordinates in a plane. This product is given as \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}, or \mathbb{R}^2, and can be visualised as a pair of axes at right-angles to each other in 2D space. The axes themselves represent the two copies of \mathbb{R}, and any point in the space can be described using an ordered pair of values, one from the ‘x’ copy of the set and one from the ‘y’ set.
